q: The AI Act is a regulation, yet its enforcement stalled in several Member States during 2025-26. The reason was that:
a: national parliaments still had to transpose the Regulation into domestic law before it could bind providers
b: Member States must designate and resource notifying and market surveillance authorities, and many did so late
c: the Court of Justice suspended the Regulation's application pending a challenge to its chosen legal basis
d: the Regulation's prohibitions were held in abeyance until harmonised standards were cited in the Official Journal
explain: A regulation applies directly, but Chapter VII still requires each Member State to designate and equip notifying and market surveillance authorities; by 2026 only a minority had both in place. Transposition is not the issue — a regulation needs none, unlike NIS2.

sources.quote: Each Member State shall establish or designate as national competent authorities at least one notifying authority and at least one market surveillance authority for the purposes of this Regulation.

the delayed availability of standards, common specifications, and alternative guidance and the delayed establishment of national competent authorities lead to challenges that jeopardise the effective entry into application of those obligations

q: The Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, entered into force on 27 July 2026. Its central effect on the AI Act was to:
a: repeal the high-risk chapter and put a voluntary conformity scheme in its place for Annex III systems
b: transfer enforcement of the general-purpose AI chapter from the Commission to national market surveillance authorities
c: defer application of the high-risk obligations while leaving the prohibitions and the general-purpose AI chapter in place
d: bring the transparency obligations for synthetic content forward so that they applied from the date of entry into force
explain: The Omnibus pushed Annex III obligations to 2 December 2027 and Annex I to 2 August 2028, while Article 5 and Chapter V continued to apply. Deferral is not repeal: conformity assessment remains mandatory once the new dates arrive.

sources.quote: Chapter III, Sections 1, 2, and 3, with the exception of Article 6(5), shall apply from: (i) 2 December 2027 as regards AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(2) and Annex III; and (ii) 2 August 2028 as regards AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(1) and Annex I;
This Regulation shall enter into force on the third day following that of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union.

q: Besides Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 itself, the Digital Omnibus on AI amended:
a: the Cyber Resilience Act (EU) 2024/2847 and the NIS2 Directive (EU) 2022/2555
b: the EASA Basic Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 and the Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230
c: the Digital Services Act (EU) 2022/2065 and the Digital Markets Act (EU) 2022/1925
d: the Data Governance Act (EU) 2022/868 and the Data Act (EU) 2023/2854
explain: Articles 2 and 3 of Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 amend the EASA Basic Regulation, so that acts on AI safety components take the AI Act's high-risk requirements into account, and the Machinery Regulation, which moves to Section B of AI Act Annex I and must absorb AI health-and-safety requirements through delegated acts applying by 2 August 2028. The data and platform acquis was not touched by this instrument.

sources.quote: amending Regulations (EU) 2024/1689, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2023/1230 as regards the simplification of the implementation of harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Digital Omnibus on AI)
it is appropriate to move to a sectoral approach by moving Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 from Section A to Section B of Annex I to Regulation (EU) 2024/1689

q: The 'small mid-cap' category now referred to in the AI Act:
a: was defined in Commission Recommendation (EU) 2025/1099 and applied to the AI Act by the Digital Omnibus
b: was created by the AI Act itself and covers any provider employing fewer than 250 persons in the Union
c: was introduced by the Data Act and determines which providers get priority access to regulatory sandboxes
d: applies only to providers of general-purpose AI models that stay below the systemic-risk compute threshold
explain: The category comes from the Commission's 2025 simplification agenda — an enterprise that is not an SME, employs fewer than 750 people and stays under €150 million turnover or €129 million balance sheet — and reached the AI Act only through Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. Fewer than 250 employees is the SME ceiling, not the small mid-cap one.

sources.quote: “small mid-cap enterprise” or “SMC” means a small mid-cap enterprise as defined in point (2) of the Annex to Recommendation (EU) 2025/1099;

it is necessary to introduce definitions for SMEs and SMCs, which should correspond to the definition set out in the Annex to Commission Recommendation 2003/361/EC (6) and Annex to Commission Recommendation (EU) 2025/1099 (7), respectively.

q: A manufacturer wants to use sensor data from machines it has sold to train a predictive-maintenance model. The instrument that most directly governs whether the machines' users can obtain that same data is:
a: the Data Governance Act, which sets the conditions for re-use of protected public sector data holdings
b: the AI Act, which requires providers of high-risk systems to use relevant and representative training data
c: the Data Act, which gives users of connected products access to the data they generate and rights to share it
d: the GDPR, which lets data subjects obtain personal data concerning them in a structured machine-readable format
explain: The Data Act's core right, applicable since 12 September 2025, is user access to connected-product data and onward sharing with third parties of the user's choice. Portability under the GDPR is the closest alternative but covers only personal data of the data subject, whereas machine telemetry is largely non-personal industrial data.

sources.quote: Where data cannot be directly accessed by the user from the connected product or related service, data holders shall make readily available data, as well as the relevant metadata necessary to interpret and use those data, accessible to the user without undue delay

Upon request by a user, or by a party acting on behalf of a user, the data holder shall make available readily available data, as well as the relevant metadata necessary to interpret and use those data, to a third party without undue delay

q: The Data Act's chapter on data-processing services obliges providers to:
a: keep all data belonging to customers established in the Union stored and processed on Union territory
b: obtain authorisation from the national market surveillance authority before offering services in a Member State
c: notify the Commission of every processing operation carried out on behalf of a public sector customer
d: remove contractual, commercial and technical obstacles to switching, and phase out switching charges
explain: Switching and interoperability are the Data Act's answer to cloud lock-in, with switching charges withdrawn after a transition period. Data localisation was deliberately not adopted — the Act addresses portability, and separately restricts unlawful third-country access to non-personal data held in the Union.

sources.quote: In particular, providers of data processing services shall not impose and shall remove pre-commercial, commercial, technical, contractual and organisational obstacles, which inhibit customers from:
From 12 January 2027, providers of data processing services shall not impose any switching charges on the customer for the switching process.

a: a notification regime for data intermediation services and a voluntary register of recognised data altruism organisations
b: a right for users to access the data generated by the connected products they own, rent or lease
c: a single European register of all personal data processing carried out by public sector bodies
d: mandatory open licensing of every category of public sector information held by national administrations
explain: The DGA is the trust framework: neutral intermediaries, altruistic data donation, and conditions for re-using protected public sector data. Connected-product access rights belong to the Data Act, adopted a year later, which is the usual confusion.

sources.quote: a notification and supervisory framework for the provision of data intermediation services; (c) a framework for voluntary registration of entities which collect and process data made available for altruistic purposes
Each competent authority for the registration of data altruism organisations shall keep and regularly update a public national register of recognised data altruism organisations.

q: Common European data spaces are best described as:
a: certified cloud regions in which service providers must host all data originating within the Union
b: national data registers that Member States are required to notify to the Commission under the Data Act
c: sector-specific federated ecosystems in which participants share data under common governance and interoperability rules
d: centralised Union repositories into which sectoral data is pooled and which the Commission operates under a single access regime
explain: Data spaces are federated by design: data stays with its holders and is shared under agreed rules, with the European Health Data Space the first one put into legislation. There is no central Commission-run pool — that model was rejected as unworkable for sensitive sectoral data.

sources.quote: common European data spaces, namely purpose- or sector-specific or cross-sectoral interoperable frameworks of common standards and practices to share or jointly process data
the Commission proposed establishing domain-specific common European data spaces for data sharing and data pooling

q: For a research team seeking EU-wide health data to train a clinical model, the European Health Data Space matters mainly because it:
a: obliges hospitals to publish anonymised patient records in an openly accessible repository from 2027
b: removes the need for a lawful basis under data-protection law where the purpose of processing is research
c: makes approval by a research ethics committee sufficient for cross-border transfers of clinical records
d: creates a permit-based secondary-use regime run by health data access bodies, phased in from around 2029
explain: The EHDS builds a governed route to secondary use: applicants ask a health data access body for a data permit, with the main secondary-use provisions applying from around 2029. It does not displace data-protection law, which continues to apply alongside it.

sources.quote: health data holders should make the data they hold available on the basis of a data permit or a health data request. For the purpose of processing electronic health data for secondary use, one of the legal bases referred to in Article 6(1), points (a), (c), (e) or (f), of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 in conjunction with Article 9(2) thereof is required.
Chapter IV shall apply from 26 March 2029. However, Article 55(6), Article 70, Article 73(5), Article 75(1) and (12), Article 77(4) and Article 78(6) shall apply from 26 March 2027

q: A very large platform runs a recommender system driven by a large model. The division of labour between the DSA and the AI Act is that:
a: both apply, but the DSA prevails as lex specialis for any service designated as very large
b: the DSA governs the platform's systemic risks and recommender transparency, while the AI Act governs the AI system as a product
c: the AI Act applies to the model and displaces the DSA obligations in respect of that part of the service, which is treated as a product
d: the DSA reaches only content moderation decisions, leaving recommender systems entirely to the AI Act
explain: The two act cumulatively on different objects: service-level duties under the DSA, product-level duties under the AI Act. Neither displaces the other, so one recommender can be a DSA systemic-risk factor and an AI system within the AI Act's scope at the same time.

sources.quote: thereby complementing obligations for providers of intermediary services that embed such systems or models into their services regulated by Regulation (EU) 2022/2065

Providers of very large online platforms and of very large online search engines shall diligently identify, analyse and assess any systemic risks in the Union stemming from the design or functioning of their service and its related systems, including algorithmic systems
